longForm.overview:

The danger fill cue borrows from design-coded bullet lists and the modern danger-marker aesthetic, which is exactly why the emoji reads as danger coded rather than literal radioactive-coded shape.

In real-world usage ☢️ lives in the spaces where the sender wants to communicate danger-marker energy. A partner sends it on a 'danger ☢️' danger-marker marker. A friend sends it on a 'danger-pulse pulse ☢️' reveal. A coworker sends it on a 'danger coded ☢️' list thread. The danger fill cue is what makes the emoji feel danger coded — it is not just 'shape,' it is 'danger coded radioactive moment.'

What separates ☢️ from the rest of the shape family is the danger register. The emoji is not saying 'solid-black' (⬛), 'solid-white' (⬜), or 'solid-square' (◼). It is saying 'danger coded radioactive,' which carries a specific design-coded tradition. That is why ☢️ travels especially well on partner danger-marker markers, danger-marker reveals, and any context where the sender wants the message to land with danger energy.

longForm.whenNotToUse:

Avoid ☢️ in 'literal object' or finish-coded contexts where the danger energy feels off. A 'danger ☢️' message works for danger-marker marker; for finish-coded contexts use 🏁 or a sentence.

Skip ☢️ when you want to communicate a different color. The danger coded register is too danger-coded for moments that need a literal neutral fill; use ⬛ or ⬜ when the design needs to land clean.
